articles.body:
El presidente, que tiene un 49% frente al 51% del senador, según Datafolha, defiende bajar la edad penal a 16 años para crímenes graves

Avanza el calendario, ya queda poco más una semana para las elecciones más reñidas de Brasil, pero la foto es, prácticamente, la misma de los últimos meses: un férreo empate técnico. La encuesta Datafolha divulgada este jueves muestra un ligero avance del presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, que recorta de cuatro a dos puntos la ventaja que le lleva Flávio Bolsonaro, el favorito. El senador ultraderechista logra un 51% de los votos válidos frente al 49% del presidente. Otra encuesta, la de Quaest, mostró la víspera la misma foto con otros números: 47% frente a 45%. La campaña de Lula acusa a la tecnológica Meta de favorecer a Bolsonaro tanto en WhatsApp como en Instagram.

La izquierda protagoniza una movilización inédita desde que el domingo llenó la avenida Paulista, en São Paulo, con una marea roja. En los días siguientes reunió grandes multitudes en Río de Janeiro y otras ciudades. La campaña digital también se ha intensificado, con la incorporación de muchos jóvenes influencers de la órbita progresista. Y el presidente sigue con sus anuncios de medidas de impacto, como un pago único de 5.000 reales (casi mil dólares) a cada microemprendedor o autobús gratuito los fines de semana.

El presidente se mostró partidario de reducir la mayoría de edad penal de los 18 años a los 16 para los crímenes más graves, incluido el homicidio, el robo seguido de muerte y la violación, entre otros, según explicó en una entrevista esta noche en Globo. Su rival plantea una reducción generalizada a los 16 y en los casos más graves a los 14.

Lula también admitió que la responsabilidad por los resultados electorales es suya. “Mire, yo soy el gobierno. Si no logré hacerme entender sobre el Gobierno que llevé a cabo, no puedo culpar a nadie; la culpa es mía”, afirmó.

Por otro lado, el equipo del candidato izquierdista denuncia que, desde que empezó la campaña, “las cuentas del presidente Lula en las plataformas de la empresa [Meta] han sufrido fallos técnicos” que le han perjudicado. La tecnológica, encabezada por Mark Zuckerberg y propietaria de Instagram, Facebook y WhatsApp, es acusada por el Partido de los Trabajadores de favoritismo en beneficio del candidato Bolsonaro.

Los internautas descubrieron este miércoles que la inteligencia artificial de WhatsApp favorecía descaradamente al heredero del clan Bolsonaro. Cuando se le pedía que elaborara un cartel electoral a favor de Lula, respondía: “No pude generar la imagen que pediste”. Y, en cambio, la misma petición sobre Bolsonaro se traducía en segundos en la entrega de un cartel con las características solicitadas.

La cúpula del Tribunal Superior Electoral se reunió este jueves en Brasilia con varios ejecutivos de Meta. Estaban tanto el juez Kassio Nunes Marques, que preside la corte que resuelve las disputas relacionadas con los comicios, y el vicepresidente, el magistrado André Mendonça. El tribunal electoral ha exigido a Meta que “promueva la igualdad de condiciones entre los candidatos para que el elector pueda elegir libremente”, según una nota difundida por la corte. Uno de sus jueces dictaminó que la empresa sea multada si no garantiza la neutralidad entre los candidatos del PT y del Partido Liberal.

Meta se comprometió con el TSE a “realizar los esfuerzos necesarios para impedir la promoción de contenidos de propaganda electoral, ya sea mediante el pago con moneda extranjera o por parte de simpatizantes”, añade el comunicado.

Estas elecciones están marcadas por el empate técnico y también por la batalla judicial paralela que libran las campañas de los candidatos y las decisiones a menudo contradictorias de distintos magistrados.

Volviendo a la última encuesta, la de Datafolha, traza el mapa territorial y sociológico donde cada uno de los dos tiene ventaja. Bolsonaro, el hijo mayor del expresidente encarcelado Jair Bolsonaro, le saca diez puntos a Lula en la región sudeste, donde vive el 40% de los brasileños. También lidera por 33 puntos entre los evangélicos, por 15 entre la clase media y por 12 entre el electorado masculino.

Lula lleva en cambio la delantera por 29 puntos en el nordeste, durante tierra natal, de 20 puntos entre los menos instruidos, de 15 entre los más pobres, de 10 entre los católicos y de nueve entre las mujeres.

La campaña de Lula tenía previsto reunirse este jueves por la tarde en Brasilia con la OEA (la Organización de los Estados Americanos) y otros organismos con misiones de observación electoral para transmitirles sus quejas sobre lo que ocurre en la esfera digital de la campaña electoral. La campaña de Lula denuncia que “Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) obtiene casi el triple de interacciones, pese a tener un 17% menos de seguidores que el presidente Lula”, según una nota de la candidatura del presidente. La compañía de Zuckerberg atribuye la sucesión de incidentes a fallos técnicos.

Otros de los sucesos que han disparado las sospechas entre las filas de la izquierda son enumeradas por la campaña de Lula: “La suspensión temporal de la cuenta publicitaria; la disminución del recuento de visualizaciones de publicaciones de apoyo a la candidatura; el bloqueo durante 24 horas de la promoción de publicaciones en el feed de Instagram; y, más recientemente, diferencias de trato en la inteligencia artificial y en las búsquedas de WhatsApp”.

Todo ello es capital porque las redes sociales se han erigido en el principal campo de batalla entre los candidatos. A falta de un debate cara a cara hasta ahora, es uno de los principales escenarios para buscar votos.

De todos modos, ni Lula ni Bolsonaro descuidan la calle. Ambos apuran las horas con unas agendas intensísimas. Este domingo está previsto que por fin celebren el primer debate de esta campaña, que será televisado en directo por el canal Band.

articles.title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
articles.summary: France's prime minister has suggested that student anger is being weaponised, as the unions and other protesters prepare to take to the streets too.
articles.preview: The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe. Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs. For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets. This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
articles.body:
The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.

Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.

For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.

This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.

Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.

France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.

The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.

Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.

The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.

"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.

So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?

Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.

Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?

"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.

She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.

"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."

"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.

"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."

"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.

Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.

But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.

France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.

I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.

They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.

"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."

None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.

The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.

- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger

- Published8 October

They are part of a defiant French tradition.

Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."

("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")

Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."

Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.

Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.

This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.

France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.

Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.

At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.

"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."

Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the Âbiggest general strike in French Âhistory. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.

Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.

"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.

"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.

But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.

Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.

For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's â¬11bn contribution to the EU's budget.

There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.

France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Persian Gulf.

Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.

In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.

Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.

But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.

"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.

"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."

For France to progress, she says, that has to change.

The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."

In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.

"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."

Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.

She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.

Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".

"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."

I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."

"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."

"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."

It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.

But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

articles.title: Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US senators and election offices
articles.summary: A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana.
articles.preview: Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US. The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received. Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.
articles.body:
Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US.

The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received.

Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.

Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail.

The suspicious letters were sent to at least five Democratic senators' offices, most of which were intercepted before delivery.

They include California's Alex Padilla, Connecticut's Chris Murphy and New York's Kirsten Gillibrand, the senators' offices confirmed to the BBC.

New York Senator Chuck Schumer and Delaware Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester were also sent the suspicious pieces of mail, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

"This incident is a stark reminder of the very real danger facing those who serve the public and who help administer our elections in the face of increasingly hostile political rhetoric," Padilla said in a statement to the BBC.

Several state offices have also received the suspicious mailings.

Delaware's Department of Elections said its office received and opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Thursday, adding that staff followed security protocols on handling suspicious mail.

The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder.

The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it.

The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC.

"This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday.

The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.

Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages.

A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.

articles.title: La dura negociación sobre el presupuesto de la UE amenaza el acuerdo antes del superaño electoral en Europa
articles.summary: El presidente del Consejo, António Costa, se hace cargo de una negociación con posiciones muy enconadas
articles.preview: El presidente del Consejo, António Costa, se hace cargo de una negociación con posiciones muy enconadas La pelea sobre el presupuesto que va a marcar las políticas de la UE en los próximos siete años se está encarnizando. Las discrepancias entre los llamados frugales, con Alemania a la cabeza, que abogan por el tijeretazo, y los amigos de la cohesión, entre ellos, España e Italia, que piden más dinero, amenazan con encallar un acuerdo sobre el marco financiero plurianual antes de final de año.
articles.body:
El presidente del Consejo, António Costa, se hace cargo de una negociación con posiciones muy enconadas

La pelea sobre el presupuesto que va a marcar las políticas de la UE en los próximos siete años se está encarnizando. Las discrepancias entre los llamados frugales, con Alemania a la cabeza, que abogan por el tijeretazo, y los amigos de la cohesión, entre ellos, España e Italia, que piden más dinero, amenazan con encallar un acuerdo sobre el marco financiero plurianual antes de final de año. Todo ello, en un clima políticamente muy tenso y en vísperas de un superaño electoral que, en realidad, se adelanta con los comicios de noviembre en España. “Honestamente, no tenemos prisa. Los ciudadanos suecos no son el cajero automático de la UE”, ha lanzado el primer ministro sueco, Ulf Kristersson, que aboga por el hachazo al presupuesto, este jueves en Bruselas. “Estamos con una propuesta claramente insuficiente”, ha advertido, por su parte, el presidente español, Pedro Sánchez.

El marco financiero plurianual (MFF, por sus siglas en inglés) es una declaración de prioridades políticas de la UE: marca en qué y cómo se va a gastar el dinero durante siete años, en este caso entre 2028 y 2034. La Comisión Europea presentó el año pasado un proyecto que ya contenía algunos recortes a las partidas tradicionales de la Política Agraria Común (PAC) y de Cohesión y elevaba otras que han sido señaladas como prioridad ante la situación geopolítica actual: defensa, seguridad y, sobre todo, competitividad, para ayudar a las empresas europeas en una carrera que ahora ganan por goleada Estados Unidos y China. Y sobre esa propuesta ha trabajado Irlanda (país que preside el semestre) en los últimos meses para lograr acercar posturas entre todas las capitales.

No lo ha conseguido. La plataforma negociadora que presentó Dublín el sábado pasado, con un recorte agregado del presupuesto del 8%, se queda en 1,62 billones de euros. Pero eso no gustó a nadie. A los frugales el recorte les pareció insuficiente y desequilibrado, ya que se ha cebado mucho más sobre el apartado de Competitividad que sobre Cohesión. Mientras, para los amigos de la cohesión, se recorta la ambición; y la Comisión Europea considera que se ha avanzado muy poco sobre nuevas fuentes de ingresos para este presupuesto. Tampoco ha gustado el proyecto irlandés al Parlamento Europeo.

Ahora se hace cargo de coordinar la negociación el presidente del Consejo Europeo, António Costa. “Nuestro objetivo sigue siendo lograr un acuerdo antes de fin de año”, ha señalado el portugués en la red social X. Y para lograrlo, Costa ha preparado un rally de cumbres de aquí a final de año: dos en noviembre y una más en diciembre.

Now discussing the EU’s next long-term budget.

Our objective remains to reach an agreement by the end of this year. Today’s discussion will bring us closer to that goal.

La explicación de la urgencia por cerrar el acuerdo presupuestario un año antes de que entre en vigor es que estas cuentas cambian mucho la estructura sobre las anteriores y las administraciones que las van gestionar (europea, nacional, regionales) necesitarán tiempo para prepararse.

Pero hay una razón menos confesable: Francia celebra elecciones presidenciales en abril y a nadie se le oculta que con la extrema derecha en El Elíseo será mucho más difícil el acuerdo. Y después habrá elecciones en Polonia, Italia y Finlandia. Un calendario que dificulta a los gobiernos moverse de sus posiciones de partida por el riesgo de perder votos. Y eso advertía este jueves uno de los ponentes en el Parlamento Europeo para estos presupuestos, el popular Sigfrid Muresan, que apuntaba que si no hay pacto antes de acabar 2026 las opciones se cierran hasta diciembre del año que viene por el calendario electoral.

Pero esa advertencia no ha servido para que se mueven las posiciones de momento. La dura postura del sueco Kristersson era secundada por su colega de Países Bajos, Rob Jetten: “Más importante que la velocidad, es tener un buen acuerdo y no uno malo. La propuesta de Irlanda no es lo suficientemente buena como para alcanzar un acuerdo”. Suecos y holandeses son dos de los países llamados frugales, pero el líder de este grupo es Alemania y tampoco su canciller, Friedrich Merz, ha sido más optimista.

Merz, al menos, no ha presionado con el calendario. “Me gustaría que pudiéramos llegar a un acuerdo antes de que termine el año”, ha explicado, a su llegada a Bruselas, “aunque las posiciones dentro de la Unión Europea estén hoy [por este jueves] muy distantes entre sí”. El alemán sí que ha dejado claro, con media broma, que está dispuesto a intentar llegar a un pacto en 2026: “Nuestras posiciones estan muy alejadas, pero eso no significa que no podamos llegar a soluciones en noviembre y diciembre. No obstante, deberíamos meternos en la maleta unas cuantas camisas más de lo habitual para la reunión del Consejo de diciembre”.

articles.title: Los tres albaceas de Isak Andic y 30 testigos más desfilarán ante la jueza por el ‘caso Andic’
articles.summary: El presidente del Grupo Planeta, el CEO de Mango y otro alto directivo explicarán las últimas voluntades del empresario y sus planes sobre una fundación benéfica
articles.preview: El presidente del Grupo Planeta, el CEO de Mango y otro alto directivo explicarán las últimas voluntades del empresario y sus planes sobre una fundación benéfica Los tres albaceas designados por Isak Andic declararán este otoño ante la jueza que investiga el caso para explicar cuáles eran y hasta qué punto se cumplieron las últimas voluntades del fundador de Mango.
articles.body:
El presidente del Grupo Planeta, el CEO de Mango y otro alto directivo explicarán las últimas voluntades del empresario y sus planes sobre una fundación benéfica

Los tres albaceas designados por Isak Andic declararán este otoño ante la jueza que investiga el caso para explicar cuáles eran y hasta qué punto se cumplieron las últimas voluntades del fundador de Mango. Como personas cercanas y de la máxima confianza del empresario, también podrán dar cuenta ante la instructora de cuál era el estado de las relaciones con su hijo mayor, Jonathan Andic, en las semanas y meses previos al fallecimiento de Isak, el 14 de diciembre de 2024, en la montaña de Montserrat (Barcelona). El primogénito permanece como investigado por homicidio en una causa que, a falta de pruebas directas de lo que ocurrió durante la excursión que ambos hicieron por el Camí de les Feixades, se asienta sobre indicios.

En su último testamento, firmado en verano de 2023, Isak Andic designó como albaceas a dos directivos de Mango (el consejero delegado Toni Ruiz y el alto directivo Daniel López) y a un amigo íntimo, José Crehueras, presidente del Grupo Planeta. Andic les había comunicado su intención de constituir una fundación benéfica para agrupar y ampliar la obra social que ya desarrollaba a través de Mango. Pero su repentina muerte a los 71 años impidió que se materializase ese proyecto. Los albaceas tendrán que explicar, entre otras cosas, cuál era el alcance que el empresario pensó para esa fundación y, en particular, si implicaba (así lo sospechan los investigadores) despojar al hijo mayor de una parte del patrimonio.

En juego está aclarar si, como sospechan la Fiscalía y la jueza, Jonathan Andic tenía un móvil económico para acabar con la vida de su padre. Tras el fallecimiento, él y sus hermanas, Judith y Sarah, se repartieron a partes iguales el imperio Mango, tal como quedó establecido en ese último testamento. La defensa confía en que los testigos acreditarán que Isak Andic en ningún momento pensé en “desheredar” a su hijo, tal y como llegó a insinuar, en su declaración, quien fue pareja del empresario en los últimos años de su vida, Estefanía Knuth.

Los albaceas mantuvieron un escrupuloso silencio en torno a la muerte de Isak Andic hasta octubre de 2025, cuando este diario reveló que la investigación apuntaba al primogénito como sospechoso de homicidio. En una carta publicada en el diario La Razón, Ruiz, López y Crehueras afirmaron que el testamento de Isak se había “cumplido de forma escrupulosa” y denunciaron que el “debate público” en torno a su muerte había causado “un mayor sufrimiento” a su entorno, incluida la familia. Los albaceas salieron en defensa de Jonathan Andic y pidieron respeto a la presunción de inocencia. “Resulta especialmente grave que se señale públicamente a una persona (...) es una peligrosa vulneración de garantías fundamentales”.

La carta se apoyaba en una nota de prensa, difundida por el Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Cataluña, en la que se afirmaba que la instrucción no se dirigía contra ninguna persona concreta. Los hechos conocidos más tarde chocan con el contenido de esa nota. Porque para entonces, los Mossos, la fiscal y la jueza ya consideraban a Jonathan Andic como objeto de investigación. El 19 de mayo de 2026, el primogénito fue detenido y la jueza ordenó su ingreso en prisión, que éste logró esquivar con el pago de la fianza impuesta, de un millón de euros.

El entrenador, el hermano, el amigo

Además de los albaceas, en diversas semanas de octubre y noviembre está prevista la declaración de otras 29 personas, cuyo testimonio debería ayudar a esclarecer tanto las circunstancias en torno a la muerte de Isak Andic como, también, sus planes con la fundación y las relaciones con su hijo. La jueza ha acordado las testificales tanto a petición de la fiscal del caso, Teresa Yoldi, como del abogado de Jonathan, el penalista Cristóbal Martell.

Entre los citados hay seis agentes de los Mossos d’Esquadra, dos de ellos especialistas en montaña, que han inspeccionado de forma reiterada la zona del Camí de les Feixades desde donde Isak Andic cayó por un barranco a más de cien metros de altura. También desfilarán ante la jueza de Martorell Raquel Nieto dos miembros del Servicio de Emergencias Médicas (SEM) que atendieron a Jonathan Andic después de que, al mediodía, éste llamara al 112. Está prevista, igualmente, la declaración de tres bomberos y del agente que ejerce como vigilante de guardia municipal de Collbató, el municipio al que pertenece el sendero de Montserrat donde se produjo el siniestro.

Los seis testigos solicitados por la defensa para tratar de desacreditar el móvil económico también han sido acordados por la jueza: el abogado Miquel Roca y su hermano Joan Roca, quienes recibieron el encargo de constituir una fundación que, según la defensa, contaba “con el apoyo y compromiso de los hijos; Ariel Sultán, el notario de confianza de Isak Andic y conocedor de todos sus testamentos; así como Raquel Delgado, directora financiera de Punta Na (la sociedad patrimonial de la familia Andic), Germán Castejón, que ayudó a “dibujar con Isak Andic” la planificación de la futura gestión del patrimonio el propio Toni Ruiz, consejero delegado y propietario del 5% de Mango, además de ser uno de los tres albaceas.

La jueza ha citado igualmente a otros testigos, incluidos dos colaboradores de la defensa, incluido el detective Francisco Marco (que ha cuestionado la investigación de los Mossos) y quien fue portavoz de la familia, Iñaki Ortega. También declararán miembros del servicio personal de la familia, cargos de Mango y personas muy cercanas al empresario: un hombre identificado como David, entrenador personal de Isak Andic; su buen amigo Isak Halfon que conoce su trayectoria desde los comienzos de Mango; o su hermano y cofundador de Mango Narman Andic.

articles.summary: Da Fatherland di Paweł Pawlikowski a Il tempo di Anne di Lisa Azuelos. Le recensioni della stampa straniera
articles.preview: Una brillante Sandra Hüller interpreta Erika Mann, la figlia dello scrittore Thomas Mann che accompagna il padre in un viaggio dalla California (dove il Nobel si è rifugiato prima della seconda guerra mondiale) alla Germania devastata del 1949, per ritirare dei premi. Fanno tappa nella Germania Ovest alleata, poi nella Germania Est occupata dai sovietici. Il viaggio dei Mann, tra discorsi e premiazioni, illustra chiaramente le sfide che perfino le visioni più illuminate dell’umanità dovettero affrontare dopo l’inferno della seconda guerra mondiale.
articles.body:
Una brillante Sandra Hüller interpreta Erika Mann, la figlia dello scrittore Thomas Mann che accompagna il padre in un viaggio dalla California (dove il Nobel si è rifugiato prima della seconda guerra mondiale) alla Germania devastata del 1949, per ritirare dei premi. Fanno tappa nella Germania Ovest alleata, poi nella Germania Est occupata dai sovietici. Il viaggio dei Mann, tra discorsi e premiazioni, illustra chiaramente le sfide che perfino le visioni più illuminate dell’umanità dovettero affrontare dopo l’inferno della seconda guerra mondiale. Pawlikowski, in un’opera in bianco e nero che riesce a dimostrare intelligenza e bellezza cinematografica in metà del tempo (82 minuti) di opere di altri autori affermati, crea una tragedia dell’esilio che in definitiva non riguarda un autore anziano o la sua famiglia, ma tutti noi, che viviamo in un mondo che non riconosciamo più. Né allora né, visti i tempi, oggi.

Nicolas Rapold, Sight&Sound

Polonia / Germania / Francia / Italia 2026, 82’. In sala

Francia 2026, 105’. In sala

Diciassette anni dopo Lol, Lisa Azuelos firma il seguito di quella fortunata commedia. La regista mette da parte Lola, il personaggio principale del primo film, per concentrarsi sulla sorella più piccola, Louise (Alessandrin), che oggi ha 25 anni. Sconvolta da una dolorosa rottura sentimentale, aggravata da una delusione professionale, Louise torna a casa dalla madre Anne, anche questa volta interpretata da Sophie Mar-ceau. Una madre un po’ fuori dal mondo che fatica a stare al passo con i tempi e che vuole godersi la ritrovata libertà, passando da un amante all’altro, ma deve fare i conti con i figli: Louise, ma anche Théo (Victor Belmondo) che le annuncia che presto diventerà nonna. Azuelos rivisita la ricetta del primo film con qualche ingrediente di attualità (social, influencer, inclusività e app d’incontri). L’aggiornamento funziona fino a un certo punto, però Il tempo di Anne rimane una piacevole riproposizione della formula originale che non si prende troppi rischi.

Olivier Delcroix, Le Figaro

Francia 2025, 80’. In sala

La bambola

Anche solo per la sua fantasiosa premessa – la bambola sessuale Audrey che una sera si risveglia davanti al suo “proprietario” – l’opera prima di Sophie Beaulieu merita di essere vista. In Barbie di Greta Gerwig la celebre bambola era convinta che il mondo fosse meraviglioso, prima di scoprirne il lato oscuro. Audrey sbarca nella società senza preconcetti, scopre i codici che la regolano, fa domande assurde e sconvolge tutti. Poi, un giorno dopo l’altro, la vita da casalinga la logora e il suo sorriso si spegne. Certo, La bambola avrebbe potuto essere più feroce, invece preferisce smontare i luoghi comuni con delicatezza.

Clarisse Fabre, Le Monde

Stati Uniti 2026, 110’. In sala

L’acclamato documentarista Lance Oppenheim ha sfornato un thriller drammatico, eccessivo e un po’ pesante che, nonostante un’elaborata atmosfera, non sembra sicuro di cosa voglia dire su mass media, moralità o qualsiasi altra cosa. Lo spunto è il controverso reality To catch a predator, andato in onda tra il 2004 e il 2008, in cui gli autori, fingendosi dei minorenni, attiravano presunti predatori sessuali in “case-trappola” dove venivano smascherati e consegnati alla polizia, dando vita a momenti televisivi di grande effetto. Mettendo da parte gli aspetti legali che seguivano la messa in onda, il film sembra preoccuparsi più che altro delle beghe che emergono dietro le quinte. Pattinson è convincente nel ruolo del pomposo conduttore dello show, Merritt Wever interpreta Andie Bender, una cinica dirigente televisiva (che è personaggio fittizio), corteggiata da un altro network, e Skyler Gisondo interpreta Dan Plumb (altro personaggio fittizio), aspirante attore dall’aspetto infantile che funge da esca. La tensione sale quando tutti si rendono conto di dover fare qualcosa per mantenere alti gli ascolti. Sorgono così anche alcune intriganti ipotesi di complotto, che però non portano a nulla.

Peter Bradshaw, The Guardian

articles.body:
Traffico aereo fortemente rallentato in tutta ItaliA a causa di una serie di anomaLie alla rete di trasmissione dati a supporto dei servizi di controllo del traffico aereo sull'intero territorio nazionale. "A partire dalle ore 6:00, in considerazione del progressivo aumento del traffico aereo e del persistere delle anomalie, per continuare a garantire la massima sicurezza delle operazioni - informa l'Enav- sono state introdotte misure di regolazione dei flussi, che comportano una temporanea riduzione della capacità di gestione degli aeromobili nello spazio aereo italiano".

"Si esclude che le anomalie siano riconducibili ad attività malevole". Lo sottolinea l'Enav affermando che non c'è nè un attacco hacker nè sabotaggio dietro il guasto che sta fortemente rallentando il traffico aereo in Italia.

Le anomalie "sulla rete geografica di trasmissione dati a supporto dei servizi di controllo del traffico aereo sull'intero territorio nazionale" sono state riscontrate "nella notte", informa la nota. E "grazie all'attivazione dei sistemi di contingency previsti, Enav ha garantito fino alle ore 6:00 di questa mattina la regolare gestione del traffico aereo, senza alcuna riduzione della capacità operativa". Le verifiche tecniche, "tuttora in corso, hanno individuato l'origine delle anomalie nella rete di trasmissione dati. Enav sta lavorando per individuare le cause e ripristinare la piena operatività dei sistemi".

I disagi

All'aeroporto di Fiumicino, come nel resto d'Italia, a causa di un problema della rete di trasmissioni dati Enav, ci sono ripercussioni sui voli. Al momento, sono riscontrabili in 4 collegamenti cancellati (Milano Linate, Riyadh, Tirana e Trieste) ed in una ventina di voli ritardati tra i 15 ed i 60 minuti di attesa. Adr sta informando i passeggeri, tramite il sito, i monitor aeroportuali ed propri canali di comunicazione che "a causa di problemi tecnici ai sistemi di controllo del traffico aereo su scala nazionale, potrebbero verificarsi ritardi e cancellazioni. Si invitano i passeggeri a verificare lo stato del proprio volo con la compagnia aerea di riferimento".

Disagi negli aeroporti lombardi a causa delle anomalie alla rete che supporta i servizi di controllo del traffico aereo.

A Malpensa il tabellone delle partenze indica ritardi da mezzora a oltre due ore, mentre quelli degli arrivi sono più contenuti. Ritardi anche all'aeroporto di Linate: da venti minuti a un'ora gli arrivi, fino a più di un'ora le partenze.

Problemi anche all'aeroporto di Orio al Serio, in provincia di Bergamo, dove il Ryanair delle 6:50 per Trapani è decollato con un'ora e mezza di ritardo; un'ora e venti di ritardo anche per il volo della stessa compagnia diretto a Berlino, mentre l'arrivo del Volotea proveniente da Olbia delle 7:45 è previsto alle 11:18. "A causa di un problema tecnico sui servizi a supporto del sistema di controllo del traffico aereo Enav a livello nazionale - recita un avviso ai passeggeri pubblicato sul sito internet dell'aeroporto -, i voli in programma potrebbero subire ritardi in partenza e in arrivo".

articles.body:
One man wanders Gaza in search of somewhere to sleep, having lost his family in an Israeli bombing.

Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Every morning, Mahmoud Khalla goes to the nearby cemetery to visit the graves of the family members he lost during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

He has held on to this morning routine in the months since he buried them, imagining his family is still around.

For Mahmoud, 40, the cemetery is the resting place of some of the people he has loved the most in his life.

His wife, his three children, his parents, his two brothers and their families, his sister and her children, and other relatives had all gathered in their family home in Jabalia, northern Gaza, on December 21, 2023.

An Israeli strike then targeted the five-storey family home, destroying the building and killing all 39 people inside. Mahmoud left his home shortly before it hit and is the only one left in his family.

The siege

Mahmoud remembers that day with heartache. Israeli tanks had surrounded the area near the house in Jabalia, northern Gaza, making it dangerous for people to move around. Food was already scarce due to the ongoing Israeli siege. In the evening, Mahmoud left the house in search of provisions to feed his family.

“I told them I would go and see what was available,” he told Al Jazeera. “As soon as I had been out for about 15 minutes, I heard a huge explosion.”

“I ran back and discovered that the targeted house was ours. I was in complete shock. But I pulled myself together. With the help of a few neighbours who were still in the area, we tried to rescue anyone who might be under the rubble.”

Israeli air attacks, quadcopters and surveillance aircraft continued to target the area. It made it impossible for Mahmoud and his neighbours to search for survivors.

“A surveillance aircraft dropped a bomb on us, so we immediately ran away,” he says. “We came back the next morning.”

Ambulances and civil defence teams were also unable to reach the site that night.

With this sense of helplessness, he imagined that some of his family might still be alive under the rubble, waiting to be rescued. He felt as though he had died a thousand times that night.

The following morning, he returned to the site and called out to his family members who might be beneath the ruined home. Nobody answered, and it was at this moment he realised he had lost nearly every person he loved.

“There were five floors of rubble. It was impossible for us to pull anyone out,” he said.

Alone

That attack marked the beginning of a long period of emptiness for Mahmoud. With his home destroyed and almost all of his relatives killed or displaced to the south, he had nowhere to go.

“Even my uncles had been killed,” he says. “Their house, opposite ours, was targeted nine days before our family home. Eighteen people were killed in that attack. The rest of the family had gone south.”

Mahmoud spent the following months displaced and alone. He moved between the streets in search of somewhere to sleep for the night. It was difficult to find shelter among displaced families when he had no relation to them.

“I was sleeping in the streets, or in cars or vehicles whenever I found one that was open,” he says. “I was totally lonely and homeless.”

With no shelter at all, Mahmoud was vulnerable to Israeli attacks. The struggle for food became as urgent as the need to find somewhere safe to sleep.

“You don’t know whether a bullet will hit you, whether a rocket will come, whether you will find food or where you will sleep,” he said.

Recovering his family

After a “ceasefire” was announced for Gaza in October 2025, families began the difficult search for their missing loved ones. Nearly a year later, an estimated 8,000 people remain missing, their bodies likely under the rubble of their homes or in other locations.

Months after the “ceasefire” began and bombing decreased, Mahmoud started recovering the remains of his family members himself. They had been entombed among the remains of their home for the last 29 months.

“The feeling that my family was still under the rubble, without being buried, was very difficult,” he says. “It never left me.”

He approached the civil defence, the Red Cross and other authorities for help. But he says a severe shortage of equipment and a huge number of other families requesting assistance meant they could be of little help.

Eventually, with the help of friends and neighbours who volunteered to work alongside him, he began the heartbreaking task of recovering his loved ones himself by hand.

He began recovering the remains around May this year, in a process that took three months.

“Sometimes, we managed to recover one person in a day. Sometimes, it took two days,” he said.

The first people he found were two relatives who had been sheltering with the family. The last were his sister and her children, who had been buried together.

He buried his family members at a cemetery near Jabalia an-Nazla, in northern Gaza.

“I felt a great sense of relief when I finally buried them,” he said. “It took me three months to recover all of their remains, working day by day.”

articles.title: La vida de los palestinos es una pesadilla
articles.summary: Frente al genocidio, los bombardeos y el acoso, los palestinos de Gaza y Cisjordania resisten intentando resucitar la esperanza y preservando la memoria de lo ocurrido, como escribe Francesca Albanese en ‘La luz del despertar’, ensayo del que ‘Ideas’ adelanta un extracto

Hoy, sin embargo, solo siento ganas de decir: I have a nightmare.
articles.body:
Frente al genocidio, los bombardeos y el acoso, los palestinos de Gaza y Cisjordania resisten intentando resucitar la esperanza y preservando la memoria de lo ocurrido, como escribe Francesca Albanese en ‘La luz del despertar’, ensayo del que ‘Ideas’ adelanta un extracto

“I have a dream”, decía Martin Luther King en 1963, cuando agitaba las conciencias desde las escalinatas del monumento a Lincoln en Washington, en uno de los discursos más emblemáticos de la historia. Hoy, sin embargo, solo siento ganas de decir: I have a nightmare. O mejor dicho: We have a nightmare, porque la pesadilla no solo afecta a los palestinos, sino a todos nosotros, a cualquiera que cree que la “justicia” no es una palabra vacía.

La vida de los palestinos es una pesadilla interminable.

En Gaza oyes el ruido de los aviones, sientes el miedo de los bombardeos, el acecho de los drones –cada vez más traicioneros y sofisticados– que te siguen, te espían, te asordan y disparan. La vida cotidiana consiste en sobrevivir en tiendas de campaña desgarradas por el viento y llenas de barro. Compartir un baño con tanta gente que usarlo se vuelve imposible. Volver a una casa medio destruida por las bombas con el riesgo de que el techo se derrumbe y mate a tu familia. Afrontar el rigor del invierno –ya es el tercero desde que comenzó el genocidio–, sin ni siquiera unos libros que poder quemar para mantener a tus seres queridos, al menos a los niños y ancianos, en un lugar cálido y seguro. Solo tiendas, frías en invierno, sofocantes en los tórridos veranos. Cuántos muertos, desplazados, huérfanos, heridos, mutilados… Y los que aún no han sucumbido al asedio total que impera desde hace más de dos años están condenados a sufrir hambre y sed, a no tener derecho a una asistencia sanitaria y a una supervivencia digna.

En Cisjordania y en Jerusalén Este, los palestinos viven con el terror de despertarse en plena noche con un soldado que los apunta con un fusil a la cara, que destruye sus casas, que los amenaza, los humilla delante de sus hijos o se los lleva consigo, con sus pijamas manchados de pipí porque se han orinado encima de miedo. Mientras tanto, los colonos están cada vez más furiosos: los ataques a los pueblos, comunidades rurales, tierras, coches, ganado, están a la orden del día. Incluso en las cárceles hay casos documentados en los que se ha autorizado a periodistas y civiles israelíes a presenciar –e incluso a grabar con sus teléfonos móviles– los abusos infligidos a prisioneros palestinos, a quienes deberíamos llamar “rehenes”, dada la falta de garantías mínimas legales que caracteriza las detenciones israelíes en el territorio palestino ocupado.

Esta fragmentación territorial, legal y política es la institucionalización de la excepción; es la transformación de la precariedad en condiciones permanentes; es un sistema en el que la ocupación militar y la colonización ya no son sucesos aislados, sino un régimen consolidado en el que el control no o se ejerce con las armas sino también mediante la planificación urbanística, la burocracia, la segmentación administrativa, con la creación de categorías jurídicas diferenciadas para personas que viven en el mismo espacio pero no bajo los mismos derechos. Y después de décadas, la violencia de esta época nos indica que hemos llega do a la fase final: la del genocidio, la de la guerra de Israel contra un pueblo que hasta ahora ha resistido como ha podido.

En los últimos dos años las cosas han ido todavía a peor: el terror se ha vuelto omnipresente, cotidiano. Se trata de una pesadilla que ha alcanzado dimensiones delirantes a los ojos del mundo.

Pero es cuando todo se derrumba a nuestro alrededor, entre el horror y la esperanza, que resulta indispensable comenzar a soñar. Para no sucumbir a la oscuridad de esos días, para intentar imaginar o al menos esbozar un “después” es necesario dar sustancia a un sueño. ¿Cuál es el mundo posible? Para alcanzarlo, hay que verlo. En Palestina hay un mundo sin apartheid.

Pese al horror, el pueblo palestino continúa imaginando un futuro que, hoy, nadie le concede. El pueblo palestino sueña en rechazar la aniquilación, en declarar que, pese a todo, su destino aún no está escrito.

[El filósofo alemán] Ernst Bloch sostenía que el ser humano es aquel que se anticipa. La esperanza, según él, es un principio de la existencia, incluso antes que algo psicológico: por lo tanto, la capacidad humana de proyectarse hacia una “esperanza consciente y concreta” es una categoría de lo real. Bloch consolida filosófica mente la idea de que soñar no es evadirse de la realidad, sino plantar la primera semilla para dar vida a algo posible. Es un principio de creación, de planificación, de resistencia.

La mujer que amasa el pan bajo los drones, el maestro que sigue enseñando bajo las tiendas, la familia que planta un limonero donde el día antes había una casa, las parejas que siguen casándose y –también en el infierno de Gaza– trayendo hijos al mundo. Es ahí donde la esperanza se vuelve radical: el sueño de un mundo que persiste y que, si nos esforzamos, puede mejorar. Este sueño es el corazón palpitante de la resistencia palestina.

Soñar, desde esta perspectiva, es también una cuestión ética que nos permite afirmar la “vivibilidad” de vidas que el mundo declara prescindibles. Soñar con el futuro de Palestina significa afirmar que las vidas de los palestinos siguen estando llenas de significado e imaginar un mundo en el que nadie –ni en Palestina ni en ningún otro lugar– sea tratado como desechable nunca más.

A lo largo de 900 días de genocidio, más de 70.000 palestinos murieron en Gaza por fuego israelí, y más de mil en el resto del territorio ocupado. 20.000 eran niños. Y el número real de víctimas podría ser mayor: un estudio estimó más de 75.000 muertes violentas solo en los primeros 15 meses de guerra, un 35% más que las cifras oficiales por el mismo periodo. Y la cifra exacta de muertes por hambre, hipotermia o falta de atención médica es más difícil de registrar oficialmente, ya que muchas muertes se producen en hogares o en tiendas de campaña sin que un médico pueda certificarlas. El análisis del genocidio debe tener en cuenta la totalidad de los crímenes cometidos contra todo el pueblo palestino. Mientras tanto, con el pretexto de una guerra existencial para defenderse de los palestinos, Israel está impulsando medidas que modifican la composición demográfica, el carácter religioso y el estatus legal de Jerusalén, destruyendo con ello los restos del tejido pluralista que durante siglos la ha distinguido como un patrimonio compartido por musulmanes, cristianos y judíos.

Por eso no es exagerado decir que la vida palestina es una pesadilla: porque allí se materializa algo que no te esperas que sea real en el mismo mundo en el que nos movemos y respiramos. El hambre se materializa. La tortura se materializa. El terror se materializa. Un genocidio que destruye un pueblo no solo con bombas, sino también con sed, hambre, infecciones, palizas, violaciones, y con la aniquilación de la identidad material, cultural, económica, religiosa e incluso de la memoria. La pesadilla se ha convertido en una estructura en la que viven todos los palestinos, también los de la diáspora, obligados a asistir desde la distancia a la masacre de su propia gente. Y todo esto ocurre justo cuando las Naciones Unidas y todo el sistema internacional celebran 80 años de existencia. 80 años de cartas, convenciones, promesas de “nunca más”. De resoluciones aprobadas año tras año y violadas día tras día. Y Palestina se erige como el laboratorio en el que el colonialismo contemporáneo, el hijo adoptivo y predilecto del imperialismo capitalista militarizado, se actualiza, se refina, se pone a prueba.

Es precisamente la pesadilla que tenemos delante la que nos invita a no rendirnos, a ejercer la capacidad de vislumbrar un futuro diferente y a construirlo juntos.

Mirar de frente el presente y el pasado sin reprimir jamás el impulso de desear el futuro, sin dejar de soñar, por imposible que parezca. Mantener viva la memoria, mirar, contar, no girar la cabeza y el corazón hacia otro lado, sino encontrar la manera de compartirla con los demás.

articles.title: Come Israele scredita i giornalisti
articles.summary: Che si tratti dei reporter uccisi nella Striscia di Gaza o dei registi di Naza, i leader politici e militari israeliani ricorrono a ogni mezzo per infangare chi non si allinea alla loro narrazione
articles.preview: All’inizio di ottobre l’esercito israeliano ha pubblicato sul suo sito ufficiale in lingua inglese una lista di 170 giornalisti e operatori dell’informazione palestinesi uccisi durante la guerra nella Striscia di Gaza e considerati come “terroristi”. The press files, questo il nome della pubblicazione, si presenta come “un’indagine approfondita basata su un’ampia gamma di fonti d’intelligence, tra cui informazioni open source, documenti raccolti sul campo, interrogatori di agenti militari da parte dei servizi segreti israeliani e altro”.
articles.body:
All’inizio di ottobre l’esercito israeliano ha pubblicato sul suo sito ufficiale in lingua inglese una lista di 170 giornalisti e operatori dell’informazione palestinesi uccisi durante la guerra nella Striscia di Gaza e considerati come “terroristi”. The press files, questo il nome della pubblicazione, si presenta come “un’indagine approfondita basata su un’ampia gamma di fonti d’intelligence, tra cui informazioni open source, documenti raccolti sul campo, interrogatori di agenti militari da parte dei servizi segreti israeliani e altro”. L’obiettivo è dimostrare che queste persone si dichiaravano giornalisti, ma ricoprivano invece ruoli “all’interno delle ali militari di organizzazioni terroristiche”.

Ogni nome, accompagnato da una fotografia, è seguito da numeri identificativi, dall’organo di stampa per cui la persona “a quanto pare lavorava come giornalista”, dall’“organizzazione terroristica” di cui faceva parte (Hamas o la Jihad islamica palestinese) e dalla posizione ricoperta al suo interno. In realtà, come dimostra un’analisi del giornalista ed esperto di Gaza Muhammad Shehada su +972 Magazine, le prove usate per accusare i giornalisti comprendono pagine vuote, documenti modificati e frammenti non verificabili.

Nei 49 casi più eclatanti le prove consistono in necrologi attribuiti direttamente a Hamas o alla Jihad islamica, che rivendicano le persone morte come loro affiliati. Ma anche questo “è lungi dall’essere conclusivo”, commenta Shehada. Di questi 49, infatti, 19 non sono mai stati inseriti nella lista dei giornalisti uccisi a Gaza compilata dal Committee to protect journalists (Cpj), di cui fanno parte 191 persone. Altri 21 sono stati rimossi dopo che è stato stabilito che non erano operatori dell’informazione o che avevano svolto un ruolo attivo nei combattimenti. Solo 78 nomi sui 170 nella lista dell’esercito israeliano compaiono anche nell’elenco del Cpj e nella grande maggioranza non sono accompagnati da foto incriminanti né da altre prove a sostegno delle accuse.

Le 59 schede relegate alla fine della lista sono prive di qualunque tipo di prova o documentazione e sono integrate semplicemente da un asterisco seguito dalla dichiarazione: “sulla base di diverse fonti di intelligence”. È il caso di Anas al Sharif, noto giornalista di Al Jazeera di 28 anni, ucciso il 10 agosto 2025 in un attacco aereo israeliano mirato contro una tenda di giornalisti all’esterno dell’ospedale Al Shifa; del suo collega Ahmed al Louh, cameraman di 39 anni ucciso nel campo profughi di Nuseirat; o di Hassan Sammour, della radio Sawt al Aqsa, morto insieme a undici componenti della sua famiglia quando una bomba israeliana ha centrato la sua casa a Khan Yunis.

L’esercito israeliano considera terroristi anche i giornalisti che sono entrati in Israele il 7 ottobre 2023, durante gli attacchi condotti da Hamas, senza considerare il fatto che molti di loro si sono precipitati nei dintorni della barriera che separa i due territori per documentare quello che stava succedendo. La scheda di Mohammed Abd al Aziz al Najjar, per esempio, contiene solo una foto di lui con le dita alzate in segno di vittoria e quello che sembra un veicolo in fiamme sullo sfondo. Quanto basta per etichettarlo come “agente militare” di Hamas.

In 19 casi le prove dell’esercito israeliano consistono in foto degli individui in posa con armi o con indosso uniformi militari, oppure in immagini riprese da video pubblicati dai gruppi estremisti palestinesi. “Inutile dire che essere ritratti in divisa militare o in posa con delle armi non significa automaticamente che una persona sia un militante”, nota Shehada. Che ricorda le foto pubblicate di Lizzy Savetsky, in cui l’influencer filoisraeliana è vestita con la divisa militare, ha un fucile in mano ed è circondata dai soldati israeliani. Inoltre dei 19 palestinesi solo quattro sono inclusi nella lista del Cpj, in seguito a indagini approfondite che hanno qualificato come “infondate” le accuse israeliane.

Oltre a essere privo di credibilità, questo tentativo israeliano di diffamare l’intera categoria dei giornalisti che continuano a raccontare al mondo quello che succede dentro la Striscia di Gaza va anche contro ogni logica, conclude Shehada. Perché mai un militante pericoloso e ricercato dovrebbe mostrarsi in pubblico, rivelare la sua posizione pubblicando aggiornamenti sui social media e trasmettere in diretta davanti a una telecamera con il rischio di essere colpito da un momento all’altro? E comunque, se proprio è convinto che tutti i giornalisti di Gaza sono legati a Hamas, Israele ha una soluzione facile per risolvere il problema: far entrare i reporter stranieri nella Striscia.

I leader israeliani, però, preferiscono di gran lunga infangare il lavoro di chi si oppone alla loro narrazione dei fatti e denuncia le atrocità commesse a Gaza. E per farlo non esitano a ricorrere a mezzi oscuri e scorretti, quasi al limite del ridicolo. È quello che sta succedendo con Naza: the real story, un film online promosso dal governo israeliano che è una specie di imitazione all’inverso di Naza, il documentario che dopo tre anni di genocidio raccontato dai giornalisti palestinesi finalmente sta facendo aprire gli occhi del mondo sui crimini dell’esercito israeliano a Gaza.

Proprio come il vero Naza, girato dai registi israeliani Yuval Abraham e Rachel Szor, anche il finto documentario si basa su interviste anonime fatte sui tetti di Tel Aviv. Ma invece di raccontare come il sistema di intelligenza artificiale viene usato dai militari israeliani per uccidere i civili a Gaza, le fonti si lanciano nella difesa dell’“esercito più morale del mondo”. Riproducendo anche lo stesso stile visivo, l’obiettivo è “rivelare nel dettaglio il sistema dietro l’uccisione di massa calcolata da parte di Israele dei terroristi a Gaza”, come si legge nella sinossi ufficiale, a sua volta una distorsione del senso dell’originale. Il progetto è ospitato sul dominio nazadocumentary.com, registrato il 16 settembre, sei giorni dopo la proiezione di Naza alla Mostra del cinema di Venezia, dove ha vinto il premio speciale della giuria.

I registi di Naza. The real story sono Ariel Averbuch, avvocato e riservista dell’esercito israeliano, e Roi Danino, candidato alle prossime elezioni con il partito di destra Israel first. L’8 ottobre il governo israeliano ha annunciato che i due registi saranno premiati con uno speciale documento chiamato “certificato di riconoscimento” per il loro “contributo alla diplomazia pubblica israeliana”. Abraham e Szor invece continuano a essere attaccati e demonizzati sui mezzi d’informazione e sulla scena politica israeliana.

L’11 ottobre il primo ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu ha chiesto l’apertura di un’inchiesta contro gli esponenti delle forze di sicurezza che hanno testimoniato anonimamente in Naza, in modo da poterli perseguire penalmente per avere “danneggiato gli interessi diplomatici e di sicurezza di Israele”. Il Guardian, che ha prodotto il documentario, ricorda che “la protezione delle fonti giornalistiche costituisce un pilastro fondamentale della libertà di stampa secondo gli standard internazionali in materia di diritti umani e gli ordini di divulgazione sono ammessi solo a condizioni rigorose”. Secondo un portavoce del giornale britannico, tutte queste mosse sono un tentativo per “distogliere l’attenzione dalle questioni urgenti sollevate dal film riguardo alle uccisioni di massa di civili palestinesi a Gaza”.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Mediorientale.

articles.body:
“The Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century,” China’s foreign minister said.

China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israeli President Isaac Herzog during a meeting in Azerbaijan that Israel should stop and reverse its “forced establishment” of West Bank settlements, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement.

Wang told Herzog that China has consistently viewed the Palestinian question as the greatest historical injustice of this century, the ministry said in the statement on Friday.

Wang emphasised that the “two-state solution” is the right path to a resolution and said the immediate priority is to fully open access to the Gaza Strip so a humanitarian “catastrophe” is not allowed to spread.

Wang added that China is willing to work with the international community to push all parties to return to dialogue as soon as possible and seek a political settlement.

Wang is attending the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia, held in Baku, Azerbaijan, as the special representative of President Xi Jinping, China’s state news agency Xinhua reported.

China urges new Middle East framework

In September, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Cairo for the first time in a decade and called on Middle East countries to oppose external influence and consider reshaping the region’s security order.

Xi’s rare visit arrived as Beijing seeks to expand its influence in the region amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

The talks covered the US-Israel war on Iran, with both presidents urging “diplomatic solutions” to reach a “comprehensive agreement to end the war”, according to a statement from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s spokesperson.

In March, China criticised the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, with Beijing demanding an immediate halt to the joint attacks. Wang told his Israeli counterpart, Gideon Saar, that the attack on Iran came as negotiations between Washington and Tehran had “made significant progress, including addressing Israel’s security concerns”, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement following the start of the war.

China was Iran’s largest trading partner, buying up to 90 percent of its oil, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission. In 2021, Beijing signed a 25-year “comprehensive strategic partnership agreement” with Tehran.

At the same time, Beijing has spent the past decade cultivating closer ties with Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, and remains a top trade partner of both the US and Israel.

From Thailand to Malaysia, ASEAN leaders are embracing Min Aung Hlaing, but critics warn it emboldens a military that is still bombing civilians.

Rohingya activist says it’s unfair to send refugees back to Myanmar

Yangon, Myanmar – When Malaysia invited Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing for a visit in September, it insisted the trip did not amount to recognition. The purpose, an official said, was to address the “longstanding issue” of refugees and migrants from Myanmar in Malaysia.

But when Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Kuala Lumpur last week, the former general – whose power grab in 2021 triggered a devastating civil war – received a red carpet welcome, complete with an honour guard.

After an official luncheon on Thursday, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Myanmar was prepared to take its nationals back at its own cost, a message with appeal in a country where anti-refugee sentiment is growing. Malaysia hosts about 193,000 Myanmar nationals, most of them from the persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority.

“Because the weather is favourable, I will dispatch Navy ships to repatriate them,” Min Aung Hlaing said.

For his part, Anwar pledged to help reintegrate Myanmar into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the 11-member regional bloc that has barred Min Aung Hlaing from its high-level meetings for refusing to carry out its peace plan. Malaysia was a vocal supporter of the plan, which is known as the Five Point Consensus and calls for an end to violence and “constructive dialogue” between the warring parties.

The civil war in Myanmar is now in its fifth year and has killed as many as 100,000 people and displaced at least 3.5 million, according to monitoring groups.

“Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we … ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN,” Anwar told reporters.

Malaysia is the fifth ASEAN nation to host Min Aung Hlaing since he became president in April, after an election held in December and January, which major opposition parties were barred from participating in. In recent months, he has visited Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos.

Following his return from Malaysia, his spokesperson said Indonesia and Brunei could be next.

“Malaysia’s reversal on Min Aung Hlaing has broken a dam of opposition to the junta,” said Bridget Welsh, an honorary research associate at the University of Nottingham’s Asia Research Institute in Kuala Lumpur. She said regional leaders who have welcomed Min Aung Hlaing, despite accusations that he has committed crimes against humanity, were putting pragmatism ahead of human rights.

“It is a step back for ASEAN as an organisation, and for Myanmar,” she said. “It does not offer any concrete path to the resolution of the Myanmar crisis, and in fact, arguably worsens it by giving the military legitimacy internationally, a legitimacy it does not have in Myanmar itself.”

‘Convenience plays a part’

Min Aung Hlaing’s rehabilitation extends beyond Southeast Asia.

Since April, the former general has also visited India, China, Russia and Belarus. At each stop, he has tried to present his government as stable and “on the path to democracy”, while pitching trade and infrastructure deals.

Even the United States appears to have opened the door.

Washington has begun direct talks with Min Aung Hlaing’s government, the Reuters news agency reported last week, despite sanctions on him over human rights abuses. These include the 2017 crackdown on the Rohingya, which sent more than 700,000 people fleeing into Bangladesh and which the US has called a genocide.

Reuters said the latest talks have focused on shutting down scam centres operating from Myanmar that have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars.

Khin Zaw Win, director of the Tampadipa Institute in Yangon, said Min Aung Hlaing’s quest for international legitimacy has been aided by a coordinated push from China, India and Thailand, all of which share borders with Myanmar. The three neighbours have experienced spillover from the war, such as fighting near their borders, disrupted trade and influxes of refugees.

Khin Zaw Win said the three countries “have the biggest stakes in how Myanmar pans out” and want the military-installed government recognised. Russia and Belarus, meanwhile, are both major arms suppliers to Myanmar, and Naypyidaw has backed Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“Convenience plays a part for all of them,” he said.

The growing diplomatic recognition, however, has done little to resolve the conflict.

While Min Aung Hlaing has invited all armed groups to peace talks, fighting continues to rage across much of the country. His forces have launched offensives to retake territory lost to opposition armed rebels and ethnic armed groups in Rakhine, Chin, Kachin and Karen states and the Sagaing region. They have been aided by an intensified air campaign and a recruitment drive that has added tens of thousands to their ranks. China, too, has helped by brokering ceasefires between the military and powerful ethnic armed groups on its border.

Still, Laetitia van den Assum, a former Dutch diplomat, said the military is unlikely to regain control of the whole country.

“That would require a huge occupation army and not – as now – a garrison army that controls a particular location,” she said. “That is why Min Aung Hlaing… bets on an increasing number of temporary ceasefires in some parts of the country so that troops can be directed to areas where he wants to continue fighting”.

Van den Assum said she found it “quite surprising” that ASEAN nations are seeking Rohingya repatriation from the very man accused of orchestrating crimes against them.

Myanmar has long denied the Rohingya citizenship, so it is unclear whether it would accept them as nationals. And with much of Rakhine State – their homeland – now held by the ethnic Arakan Army, it is far from clear where they would go.

“It is the blind speaking to the blind,” she said.

‘Low-cost, high optics’

Min Aung Hlaing has made other gestures.

Shortly before his trip to Thailand in August, he allowed the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to see Aung San Suu Kyi, the civilian leader he deposed in 2021. The 81-year-old Nobel laureate has been held incommunicado since the coup, and the ICRC visit on August 3 produced her first photographs in years.

Sai Kyi Zin Soe, a research fellow at the University of Sydney, called the move a “low-cost, high-optics gesture rather than a real political opening”. The visit confirmed only that Aung San Suu Kyi is alive, “nothing more”, he said.

He noted that the military’s air raids have continued unabated even as ASEAN leaders roll out the red carpet, including a September 28 strike on a market in Rakhine State that killed an estimated 50 people.

The continuing attacks, he said, were the “strongest evidence that soft diplomacy hasn’t produced any deterrent effect”.

Sai Kyi Zin Soe also warned that the legitimacy conferred by the foreign visits would embolden the military further.

“Given the near-total absence of deterrence, no meaningful sanctions enforcement, an ASEAN pivoting toward re-engagement, and continued arms and fuel access via China and Russia, the military has every structural incentive to keep escalating, particularly in contested zones like Sagaing and Rakhine, where its grip is weakest,” he said.

Much now depends on the Philippines and Singapore, ASEAN’s current and incoming chairs.

Phil Robertson, director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates, said the two countries must set an agenda that pushes back hard on entreaties from others in the region to allow “Myanmar fully back into the fold” and keep pressing the bloc’s five-point peace plan.

He also urged the US, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and the European Union to adopt targeted sanctions, such as an aviation fuel ban, rather than leaving “the whole Myanmar conundrum” to the regional bloc.

“International accountability is now more urgent than ever, whether that comes through additional universal jurisdiction cases or some sort of breakthrough to refer Myanmar’s generals to the International Criminal Court,” he added.

Zaheena Rasheed reported and wrote from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

articles.title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says
articles.summary: Yemen's information minister says the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.
articles.preview: Five people have been killed and 16 injured in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace. The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".
articles.body:
Five people have been killed and 16 injured in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.

Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".

A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.

Yemeni health minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included "those working to guard the site and civilian employees".

The country's Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".

He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.

Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.

The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.

On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.

"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.

"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.

There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.

Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.

Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.

At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.

The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.
